name: Maya Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for seeing me. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no links to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and nothing you say will be traced back to you. So you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you describe a normal working day for me?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior solicitor at a small firm on Bridge Street, in a commuter town, and I do conveyancing, which is the legal side of buying and selling houses. A normal day is checking title documents, chasing searches from the council, answering buyers who ring every morning asking if they can move on Friday. There are six of us, and Mr Okafor, the senior partner, has been there 31 years. I like the paper files, honestly, and the moment I hand someone their keys.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The phones, and the case management system the firm brought in last year, which I still find fiddly. I'm slower than the other junior, Lena, and I know it, because I double-check everything by hand. I don't use any of those AI chat tools, I just don't trust them with someone's house. At home it's me and Tomas, my boyfriend, who's an electrician, and we're saving for our own place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, because people have been promising robot conveyancing for years. Houses are messy: boundaries, old rights of way, a seller who forgot to mention the extension. I'd say that to anyone who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still be a bit worried, just not about AI. The online conveyancing firms already charge half what we do, and Mr Okafor talks about retiring in two or three years. If he sells the firm or merges, I don't know if a slow junior like me comes with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing exactly what I do, and try to get my files done a little faster, maybe 15 completions a month instead of 12. I'd keep putting £200 a month towards the house deposit. And I'd ask Mr Okafor straight out at my review what his plans are, which I've been too scared to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not panicky, but there's a background hum of 'what if the firm closes'.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if Mr Okafor did sell?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably ask the buyer firm to keep me, and if they wouldn't, I'd look at the two other firms in town. There are a few conveyancing jobs around, not loads. I'd rather drive an hour to a firm in the next town than learn a whole new job. Conveyancing is what I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at work you'd worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pat, our secretary, who types up the letters and does the post. If even the boring AI takes over letters, Pat's hours are first to go. Pat's been there longer than I've been alive.

say: **Houses are messy**, so robot conveyancing was never coming.
People have promised **automated house sales** for years.
**Boundaries** and old rights of way still need a person to check them.
think: The real threat is **cheaper online firms**, not AI.
If the senior partner **retires** and sells, a **slow junior** may not be kept.
do: Raise my pace from **12 to 15** completions a month.
Keep saving **£200 a month** for the house deposit.
Ask about the senior partner's **retirement plans** at my review.
feel: **Uneasy**, with a background hum about the **firm closing**.
S0.quote: I'd rather drive an hour to a firm in the next town than learn a whole new job. Conveyancing is what I know.
fieldNote: Her worry in a no-change world is the **firm's future** and cheaper competitors, not technology.
She knows she is **slower** than her colleague and admits it.
She avoids risk: she'd **commute further** before retraining.

steps.text: Push from 12 to 15 house completions a month
Save £200 a month towards a house deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should be careful, because a mistake on a house purchase can cost someone their life savings. I'd tell clients they still get a real person checking their file. I wouldn't post anything, I never do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think conveyancing is right in the firing line. Checking documents, filling in forms, answering 'when's completion' emails: that's my whole day, and it's all on that card. I think the firm either buys the software and needs fewer of us, or the online firms get even cheaper and we lose clients.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd probably wait and see what Mr Okafor does before changing anything. I'd cut back a bit, stop the takeaways and the gym, maybe £150 a month, so the deposit savings can double as a safety net. And if the firm made using the new software a rule, I'd go on the training, but only because I'd have to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can feel the ground tipping, and I'm the sort who'd rather stand still and hold on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd only learn the software because you'd have to. Why not before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd be learning something that might not even last, and I learn slowly, so it costs me more than it costs Lena. I check every title deed by hand because a person's house is on it. I'm not handing that job to a chatbot until somebody makes me. I know that sounds stubborn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Tomas the evening the firm says it's cutting a junior?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's probably me, because Lena is quicker and she likes the computers. Tomas would say we'll be fine on his wage for a bit, and I'd believe him for about a day. Then I'd start looking at the job ads on my phone in bed.

say: A conveyancing mistake can cost someone their **life savings**.
Clients should still get a **real person** checking their file.
think: **Conveyancing** is right in the firing line.
The firm either buys software and needs **fewer juniors**, or loses clients.
do: **Wait** to see what the senior partner decides before changing anything.
Cut takeaways and the gym to free **£150 a month**.
Go on **software training** only if the firm makes it a rule.
S1.quote: I check every title deed by hand because a person's house is on it. I'm not handing that job to a chatbot until somebody makes me.
fieldNote: She is **resistant by temperament**, and frames it as **care** for clients.
She expects to be the **junior who goes**, because her colleague is faster.
Her partner's **steady trade** is the household's quiet safety net.

steps.text: Wait for the senior partner's decision before changing anything
Cancel takeaways and the gym to save £150 a month
Attend the firm's software training if it becomes compulsory

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's frightening and the government needs to do something, quickly. I'd probably say it at the kitchen table more than at work, because at work we'd all be pretending to be fine. I'm not one for online arguments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'm out of law within two years. Conveyancing is all thinking and paperwork, so it goes on day one. I don't have a plan for that, and I'm not someone who makes plans quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the house deposit saving and keep the money as our emergency fund, about four months of my costs. I'd ask Tomas whether his firm would take me on in the office, booking jobs and doing quotes, even though I know that's thinking work too. And I'd lean on my parents, maybe move back in with them for a while to save rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. Properly scared, the kind where you can't eat your dinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does it mean for you that robots come three years later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For three years he'd be the one paying for everything. My boyfriend Tomas has until about 2031 as an electrician, and I've got until 2028. We'd have three years before we're both in the same spot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The deposit plan, first. Then the car, because I can bus to wherever I end up. My mum's birthday trip in the spring would go too, which would upset her more than she'd say.

say: It's **frightening** and the government needs to act **quickly**.
I'd say it at the **kitchen table**, not online.
think: I'm **out of law** within two years, because conveyancing goes on day one.
I have **no plan** and I don't make plans quickly.
do: Stop the **deposit saving** and keep it as a **four-month** emergency fund.
Ask Tomas's firm about **office work** booking jobs and quotes.
Move back in with my **parents** for a while to save rent.
feel: **Scared**, the kind where I can't eat my dinner.
S2.quote: My boyfriend Tomas has until about 2031 as an electrician, and I've got until 2028. We'd have three years before we're both in the same spot.
fieldNote: She expects to lose her **job** within two years and has **no plan** ready.
The **three-year gap** before robots makes her partner the sole earner for a while.
She'd lean on **family** first: her partner, then her parents' spare room.

steps.text: Pause the house deposit and keep it as emergency money
Move back to her parents' house to save rent
Ask her boyfriend's electrical firm about office work
Sell the car and take the bus

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to plan, so the firms and the government should be planning, and telling us what they're planning. I'd say it to Mr Okafor too. Five years sounds like a lot, but conveyancing files take months each, so it's really only a few hundred files.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still lose the job, just in 2031 instead of 2028. I think I'd spend the first two years telling myself it might not happen, because that's what I do. Then I'd panic in year three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and keep saving, maybe push the savings to £300 a month by cutting holidays. Around year two I'd look at jobs where you have to be physically there: court usher, registry office, maybe a council role meeting people. I'd ask my cousin Ines, who works at the county court, what those jobs pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, if I'm honest with myself. The extra years help with money, but they don't give me a new job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd tell yourself it might not happen. Is there anything that would stop you doing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe if Tomas or my mum pushed me. When my colleague Lena starts quietly applying elsewhere, I'll know it's real. Lena always knows first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Mr Okafor?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thank you for the training and please tell me early if the firm is closing. I think he'd tell me, he's decent. I'd also ask for a reference while he still remembers who I am.

say: Firms and government should be **planning now** and telling us.
Five years is only a **few hundred files**.
think: I'd still **lose the job**, just in **2031**.
I'd deny it for **two years**, then panic in year three.
do: Raise savings to **£300 a month** by cutting holidays.
Look at **in-person jobs** like court usher or registry office around year two.
Ask my cousin at the **county court** what those jobs pay.
feel: **Alarmed**, because extra years help money but don't bring a **new job**.
S3.quote: When my colleague Lena starts quietly applying elsewhere, I'll know it's real. Lena always knows first.
fieldNote: She predicts her own **denial**, which is unusually self-aware.
Her fallback is jobs that need you **physically present**, like court usher.
Even with five years she expects to **lose the job** and feels it keenly.

steps.text: Cut holidays to save £300 a month
Ask her cousin at the county court about usher jobs
Keep conveyancing until the firm signals cuts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and lots of things people predicted ten years ago didn't happen. I'd keep my head down and do my files. If anyone asked, I'd say I'll deal with it when it comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I know that's what someone like me always says. With ten years, I'd be 37, maybe with kids, and that's a worse time to lose a job than now. But my job probably holds for the next few years, which is about as far ahead as I can think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the deposit plan going and probably buy a small place with Tomas in two or three years, because his trade will last longer. I'd maybe do one evening course, something like mediation, but only if the firm paid. Mostly I'd wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, in a slow way. It's a worry I'd carry around rather than act on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd buy a house even knowing AGI is coming. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if we wait for the future to be certain, we'll rent forever. My boyfriend Tomas is an electrician, and his trade lasts longer than mine. A mortgage taken now leans on his wage, not on my job. I'd rather lock in something now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you actually act?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Mr Okafor sold the firm, or if the online firms started taking our local clients. That would be a real thing I could see. A date in the news doesn't feel real to me.

say: Ten years is **a long time** to wait for anything.
Lots of **predictions** from ten years ago never happened.
I'll **deal with it** when it comes.
think: At **37**, maybe with kids, is a worse time to lose a job.
My job probably holds for the **next few years**.
do: Buy a **small place** with Tomas within two or three years.
Do an **evening mediation course** only if the firm pays.
Mostly **wait** for a clear sign before acting.
feel: **Anxious** in a slow way, a worry I **carry** rather than act on.
S4.quote: My boyfriend Tomas is an electrician, and his trade lasts longer than mine. A mortgage taken now leans on his wage, not on my job.
fieldNote: She plans **around her partner's trade**, trusting it to last longer than law.
She'd act only on **visible local signs**, not a date in the news.
She still worries about being **37 with children** when AGI lands.

steps.text: Buy a small house with her boyfriend within three years
Take an evening mediation course if the firm pays
Keep doing house sales until a clear local sign

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because I'd have no time and I'm slow to change. What would help is someone telling me exactly which jobs are still there, and help paying for a course into one of them. And honestly, help with rent for a year, so moving back home isn't the only option.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about people who don't like change. Everyone talks about adapting like it's easy. Some of us need someone to sit down and show us the next step, one at a time. We aren't lazy, we just need longer and more help.

headlineQuote: Everyone talks about adapting like it's easy. Some of us need someone to sit down and show us the next step, one at a time.
portrait: Maya is a **27-year-old** junior conveyancer at a **six-person firm** on Bridge Street.
She **never uses AI**, checks title deeds by hand, and knows she's **slower** than her colleague.
Her first worry is the **senior partner retiring** and cheaper online firms.
As the AGI date nears she moves from **waiting** to leaning on her **boyfriend and parents**.
She hopes for **clear guidance** and practical help, not big speeches.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she'd have no time and changes slowly.
whatWouldHelp: A clear list of **jobs still there** and help paying for a **course**.
**Rent help** for a year, so moving home isn't the only option.
